worlds.setting: The surface is an unremarkable 1990s America: federal offices, motels and small towns, a country that has officially stopped believing in flying saucers. Underneath it, the government has known since 1947 that something non-human is here, and a small group of officials has spent fifty years managing that fact in secret. The X-Files office holds the cases nobody wants filed. Knowing costs you: the record is simultaneously true and officially discredited, and the people who keep it tend to lose their careers, their families and their lives.
worlds.conflict: Mulder believes the truth is knowable and suppressed; Scully demands evidence that would survive a courtroom. Both are right. The government is in a standing arrangement with visitors it cannot fight, made by men who priced a few generations of silence as a fair trade for the species. Every case asks whether exposure would save anyone, or would end the arrangement that keeps humanity alive.
worlds.politics: Agency politics on the surface, a shadow cabinet underneath. A handful of powerful men decide what the public may know, and the Bureau's official position is that Mulder's work is a waste of money.
worlds.technology: The tech is deliberately mundane: filing cabinets, payphones, rental cars, autopsy rooms. The aliens have what we cannot build, the conspiracy has only what it can steal and reverse-engineer, and none of it reaches the public. You notice the absence of the ordinary things that would prove anything, such as a working camera or a witness who stays alive.
worlds.mood: Paranoid, melancholy, claustrophobic. It is a show about two people doing careful work in a building that has already decided the answer, and about how lonely it is to be the only one asking.

connections.note: The same hidden arrangement as farce rather than horror: both turn on what the government knows and never says.

worlds.setting: New York looks like New York: traffic, tourists, hot dog carts, a news cycle about nothing. Underneath it, roughly fifteen hundred aliens live disguised among humans, and a small agency runs their arrivals, paperwork, disputes and deportations. Both films and cartoon spin-off are consistent about one thing: the extraordinary here is administered. The surface stays beautifully ordinary because a neutral zone is only neutral while nobody notices it. The cost of knowing is exacted by machine: one flash and you lose the memory, one signature and you lose your name.
worlds.conflict: The agency's mandate is to keep Earth a neutral zone, which makes immigration control and public relations more important than firepower. Every incident that risks exposure is a catastrophe, whether a hostile alien or a human demanding proof causes it. The comedy comes from procedure; the tension from the fact that procedure is all that stands between the planet and everyone who wants it.
worlds.politics: An unofficial department with no congressional oversight, no public budget line and no accountability to anyone outside itself. It answers to no electorate, and the only check on it is its own sense of restraint.
worlds.technology: Chrome sidearms and sunglasses are the visible kit, but the real technology is discretion: neuralysers that erase memory, disguises that hide a body, doors that fold space. Nothing is designed to impress, only to be forgotten. What is missing is any interest in improving human life. The agency could change the world and has decided, for excellent reasons, not to.
worlds.mood: Deadpan, breezy, faintly sinister. A galaxy-threatening emergency is handled like a lost-luggage claim, and the joke is that this is exactly how it should be handled.

worlds.setting: Ordinary Britain in the 1990s: suburbs, comprehensive schools, the evening news, a country with no idea. Laid over the top of it is a parallel magical Britain with the same postcode, hidden behind enchantment, misdirection and memory charms. It has its own civil service, newspaper, prison, bank and class system, and it is small enough that everyone knows everyone. The cost of knowing is the cruellest of the five worlds: the Muggle side of your family is not supposed to be told.
worlds.conflict: Two wars, twenty years apart, over whether magic belongs to everyone or only to those born to it. Powerful families and the movement they fund want a pure-blood order restored; the Ministry wants calm above all else, which makes it the enemy of anyone trying to warn it. Because the world is concealed, the war is fought in spaces the ordinary one never looks at.
worlds.politics: The Ministry of Magic governs the concealed population: an elected minister, a permanent bureaucracy, a court, and one seat of contact with the Muggle Prime Minister. It is a small civil service with a small civil service's instincts, which is why it spends its worst year denying a war rather than fighting one.
worlds.technology: Magic replaces almost every modern convenience, and nothing is built: no computers, no electronics, no industry, only wands, quills, enchanted objects and a steam train to school. Wizards conjure what Muggles manufacture, treat Muggle engineering as a curiosity, and cannot easily fix a problem that magic does not solve. The result is a world with 1990s politics and medieval infrastructure.
worlds.mood: Cosy and parochial on the surface, genuinely frightening underneath. The emotional register is boarding-school warmth, petty snobbery and real grief, all in the same corridor.

Both are 1990s adolescence split between an ordinary life and a secret, lethal duty.

Both run a hidden ministry their national government half-knows about and never mentions.

worlds.setting: Sunnydale, California, late 1990s: stucco houses, a mall, a high school, a nightclub called the Bronze, and a death rate the local paper never asks about. The town sits on a Hellmouth, a weak point between worlds, which is why so much happens here and why the adults explain none of it. The show's real structure is high school as horror: the monsters are literal and the metaphors are adolescent. To know about it is to be drafted, and the drafting is lifelong.
worlds.conflict: One girl in each generation is given the strength to fight vampires and demons, and the fight never ends for her. Buffy wants an ordinary life and is not allowed one; her friends insist on helping and are always in danger because of it. The engine is that the power is real, necessary, isolating and unfair, and each season makes her pay more for it.
worlds.politics: A secret council of Watchers trains and directs the Slayer, treats her as an instrument, and controls what she is told. The town authorities, the police and the school board are innocent, corrupt or wilfully blind. Everything is informal: the real decisions are made by a teenager, her librarian and her friends.
worlds.technology: Deliberately analog and cheap: stakes, crossbows, a card index in a school library, research done by hand, and no mobile phones worth relying on. Magic exists and is expensive to use. The conspicuous absence is any adult institution that could help, and any weapon that does not have to be swung by a person at close range.
worlds.mood: Wry, adolescent, genuinely sad. The jokes land fast, the horror is practical and physical, and grief is treated as the actual cost of the job.
themes: the loneliness of the only one

worlds.setting: Not our world. Lyra's Oxford has colleges, gas lamps and a river, and the year is roughly ours, but the Reformation never broke the Church's power: John Calvin became Pope, the Magisterium still governs, and there was no scientific or industrial revolution. Every person is accompanied by a daemon, an animal-shaped soul that speaks, changes shape in childhood and settles at puberty. Power is liturgical, fuel is anbaric, and the North is a frontier of zeppelins, witches, armoured bears and experimental stations.
worlds.conflict: The Church teaches that Dust, a particle visible only to instruments and attracted to conscious beings, is evidence of original sin, and it is prepared to sever children from their daemons to prevent it. Against that stands a child whom the witches' prophecy concerns, and the question the trilogy asks is whether knowledge and desire are pollution or the whole point of being alive.
worlds.politics: The Magisterium rules Lyra's world: doctrine is law, and it has courts, spies and experimental stations of its own. Everything else sits outside it or under it, from the colleges of Oxford to the Gyptians on the canals and the witch clans of the far north, who owe the Church nothing.
worlds.technology: No electronics, no screens, no computing. Zeppelins, anbaric lamps, naphtha, hand-written reports, glass instruments and the alethiometer, a compass-like device that answers questions in symbols and is read by intuition rather than calculation. The world is industrious without being industrial: it can build airships and cannot build a radio, and it possesses photographic plates while lacking the thought that would make them mundane.
worlds.mood: Wonderful and dreadful at once. It reads as a children's adventure written in the language of theology, where the villains are sincere, the scholarship is dangerous and growing up is the most serious event in the universe.

connections.note: Turn-of-the-millennium British fantasy opposites: one affirms the hidden order, the other dismantles holy authority.
Both make the real world a managed version of a larger one, and knowledge a thing you cannot unlearn.
Both take instruments and evidence seriously, then ask what a person owes to what they cannot prove.
Mirror images: a federation built on inquiry, and a church that burned the inquiry down.
